```{r}
#| label: setup
library(ggcarto)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(maps)
library(patchwork)
```

## The workflow, in one page

ggcarto is organised around a sequence: **inspect → choose → classify → map →
diagnose**. Look at the distribution before classing it, choose the number of
classes with the trade-offs in front of you, classify with a method you can
name, draw the map, then read the decisions back off the finished map. Here it
is once, end to end, on the package's bundled data: the 217 counties of the US
Northeast as an sf object, with `geom_sf()`.

```{r}
#| label: workflow-data
library(sf)
income <- northeast_counties$median_income
```

**Inspect.** Where do the candidate methods put their breaks?

```{r}
#| label: workflow-inspect
#| fig-height: 5
compare_breaks(income, c("equal", "quantile", "fisher"), n = 5)
```

**Choose.** How many classes? `class_guide()` scores each candidate count on
fit, balance, separation and readability, and suggests one. It says
*suggested*, not *optimal*: there is no universal optimum, only a trade-off,
and the table is there so you can disagree.

```{r}
#| label: workflow-choose
class_guide(income, style = "fisher")
```

**Classify.** The classes as a table, with the labels the legend will carry.

```{r}
#| label: workflow-classify
class_summary(income, "fisher", 5,
              labels = label_map(style = "interval", prefix = "$",
                                 big.mark = ",", digits = 0, open = TRUE))
```

```{r}
#| label: workflow-plot-breaks
#| fig-height: 3
plot_breaks(income, "fisher", 5)
```

**Map.**

```{r}
#| label: workflow-map
#| fig-height: 4.6
map <- ggplot(northeast_counties) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = median_income), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", style = "fisher", n = 5,
                       range = c(0.15, 1), na.value = "grey85",
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", prefix = "$",
                                          big.mark = ",", digits = 0, open = TRUE)) +
  labs(title = "Median household income", fill = NULL) +
  theme_ggcarto(base_size = 9)
map
```

**Diagnose.** What did that scale actually decide, and what would a reader get
wrong?

```{r}
#| label: workflow-diagnose
diagnose_map(map)
```

The rest of this vignette takes each of those decisions in turn, on a second
dataset. `vignette("good-maps")` explains what each of the numbers above is
for, and what a good choropleth has beyond them.

## The data

Everything below uses `ggplot2::midwest` — 437 counties across five states, from
the 2000 census — joined to county polygons from the **maps** package. It is a
good test case precisely because its variables misbehave in different ways:
`poptotal` is dominated by one county, `percollege` is nearly normal,
`percblack` has a long thin tail.

```{r}
#| label: data
data(midwest)

# strip punctuation so "St. Clair" and "stclair" meet in the middle
norm <- function(x) gsub("[^a-z]", "", tolower(x))

mw_data <- midwest |>
  mutate(
    region = tolower(state.name[match(state, state.abb)]),
    sub    = norm(county)
  ) |>
  # a diverging variable: how far a county sits from its own state's median
  mutate(college_gap = percollege - median(percollege), .by = state)

mw_poly <- map_data("county") |>
  filter(region %in% c("illinois", "indiana", "michigan", "ohio", "wisconsin")) |>
  mutate(sub = norm(subregion)) |>
  left_join(mw_data, by = c("region", "sub"))

nrow(mw_data)
sum(is.na(mw_poly$poptotal))   # every polygon found its data
```

A helper, so the rest of the vignette is only about the scale:

```{r}
#| label: helper
mw_map <- function(scale, var = "poptotal", title = NULL) {
  ggplot(mw_poly, aes(long, lat, group = group, fill = .data[[var]])) +
    geom_polygon(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.07) +
    coord_quickmap() +
    scale +
    labs(title = title, fill = NULL) +
    theme_void(base_size = 9) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9.5, hjust = 0),
      legend.key.size = unit(8, "pt"),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 6.5)
    )
}
```

## Why this package exists

### Equal intervals lose the map

County population spans three orders of magnitude and one county — Cook,
Illinois — holds 5.1 million people. Cut that into five equal-width classes and
436 counties land in the first one.

```{r}
#| label: equal-vs-quantile
#| fig-height: 3.4
mw_map(scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", "equal", 5), title = "equal width") +
  mw_map(scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", "quantile", 5), title = "quantile")
```

```{r}
#| label: class-counts
table(cut(mw_data$poptotal, compute_breaks(mw_data$poptotal, "equal", 5),
          include.lowest = TRUE))
table(cut(mw_data$poptotal, compute_breaks(mw_data$poptotal, "quantile", 5),
          include.lowest = TRUE))
```

### ggplot2 cannot do this on its own

This is the part worth knowing even if you never use the package. ggplot2 calls
a binned scale's `breaks` function with the scale **limits** — two numbers — not
with the data. Every classification algorithm a cartographer uses needs the
distribution. So the obvious thing silently does the wrong thing:

```{r}
#| label: silent-failure
breaks_of <- function(p) {
  b <- ggplot_build(p)
  sort(unique(b$plot$scales$scales[[1]]$get_breaks()))
}

base <- ggplot(mw_data, aes(percollege, percbelowpoverty, colour = poptotal)) +
  geom_point()

# looks right, is not: ggplot2 only ever passes the limits to breaks_jenks()
breaks_of(base + scale_colour_binned(breaks = breaks_jenks(5)))

# ggcarto keeps the trained data, so jenks means jenks
breaks_of(base + scale_colour_intervals(style = "jenks", n = 5))

compute_breaks(mw_data$poptotal, "jenks", 5)
```

No warning is emitted in the first case. `ggcarto` ships a `ScaleBinnedMap`
ggproto that retains the trained values; that single fix is most of the
package's reason to exist.

## One engine, five mappings

`scale_fill_map()` and `scale_colour_map()` cover every way a variable can be
coloured. `type` is the only thing that changes.

```{r}
#| label: types
#| fig-height: 6.5
pal <- "brewer::YlGnBu"
(
  mw_map(scale_fill_map(pal, type = "continuous"), title = "continuous") +
  mw_map(scale_fill_map(pal, type = "intervals", style = "jenks", n = 6),
         title = 'intervals, style = "jenks"')
) / (
  mw_map(scale_fill_map(pal, type = "rank"), title = "rank") +
  mw_map(scale_fill_cat("brewer::Set2", na.value = "grey90"),
         var = "state", title = "categorical")
)
```

Each has a shorthand that autocompletes next to ggplot2's own scales:

| `type` | Shorthand |
|---|---|
| `"continuous"` | `scale_fill_cont()` |
| `"intervals"` | `scale_fill_intervals()` |
| `"categorical"` | `scale_fill_cat()` |
| `"ordinal"` | `scale_fill_ord()` |
| `"rank"` | `scale_fill_rank()` |

`rank` is worth a second look. It colours by position in the distribution
rather than by value, so it is immune to outliers entirely — useful as a first
pass when you do not yet know the shape of a variable. Its legend is keyed at
the quartiles rather than drawn as a bar, because a bar would place its ticks
linearly in value while the colours sit by rank — the labels would point at the
wrong colours.

## Class intervals

### The full set

```{r}
#| label: styles-table
map_styles_info()
```

### Side by side

```{r}
#| label: style-gallery
#| fig-height: 8.5
gallery <- function(styles, var, n = 5) {
  plots <- lapply(styles, function(s) {
    mw_map(scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", s, n), var = var, title = s)
  })
  Reduce(`+`, plots) + plot_layout(ncol = 3)
}
gallery(c("equal", "pretty", "quantile", "jenks", "fisher", "kmeans",
          "headtails", "box", "maximum"), var = "poptotal")
```

Note how differently they treat the same skew. `equal` and `pretty` are honest
about magnitude and show nothing. `quantile` maximises contrast but implies
differences that are not there at the low end. `jenks`, `fisher` and `kmeans`
chase gaps in the distribution and land in similar places. `headtails` is built
for exactly this shape — a heavy tail — and splits recursively above the mean.
`box` and `maximum` are diagnostic rather than presentational.

### Choosing one

| If the variable is | Try |
|---|---|
| Roughly uniform, and magnitude matters | `equal`, `pretty` |
| Skewed, and you want visible geography | `quantile` |
| Skewed with real clusters | `jenks`, `fisher`, `kmeans` |
| Heavy-tailed (populations, incomes, counts) | `headtails`, `log` |
| Roughly normal, and deviation is the story | `sd` |
| Being explored rather than presented | `box`, `maximum` |

`fisher` is the exact optimum that `jenks` approximates, and it is faster.
Prefer it unless you need to match a published `jenks` map.

### Standard deviations

`sd` puts breaks at multiples of the standard deviation either side of the
mean, which is the classic treatment for a variable read as deviation.
`step` controls the class width.

```{r}
#| label: sd
#| fig-height: 3.4
mw_map(scale_fill_intervals("brewer::RdBu", "sd", n = 6,
                            midpoint = 0, reverse = TRUE, labels = "ranges"),
       var = "college_gap", title = "sd, 1 sd classes") +
  mw_map(scale_fill_intervals("brewer::RdBu", "sd", n = 6, midpoint = 0,
                              reverse = TRUE, labels = "ranges",
                              breaks = breaks_sd(6, step = 0.5)),
         var = "college_gap", title = "sd, 0.5 sd classes")
```

### Log and geometric

```{r}
#| label: log
#| fig-height: 3.4
mw_map(scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", "log", 5), var = "popdensity",
       title = 'style = "log"') +
  mw_map(scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", "geometric", 5), var = "popdensity",
         title = 'style = "geometric"')
```

`transform` is separate from `style`: it changes where colour sits along the
ramp, while `style` decides where the class edges fall. Classification always
happens in data space, so labels stay in the units you started with.

```{r}
#| label: transform
mw_map(scale_fill_map("brewer::YlGnBu", transform = "log10"), var = "popdensity",
       title = "continuous, log10 transform")
```

## Break functions on their own

Every style is also a plain function of the data. That makes them useful well
outside this package — including inside ggplot2's own binned scales, where they
are the missing piece.

```{r}
#| label: breaks-standalone
breaks_jenks(5)(mw_data$poptotal)
compute_breaks(mw_data$percbelowpoverty, "quantile", n = 4)

# classify a column yourself
mw_data |>
  mutate(pop_class = cut(poptotal, breaks_fisher(5)(poptotal),
                         include.lowest = TRUE)) |>
  count(pop_class)
```

```{r}
#| label: breaks-elsewhere
#| fig-height: 3.2
ggplot(mw_data, aes(percollege, percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = poptotal), size = 1.6) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_binned(
    breaks = breaks_quantile(5)(mw_data$poptotal),   # note: pre-computed
    type = "viridis"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(9)
```

The `(mw_data$poptotal)` there is not a typo. Passing the *function* to a plain
ggplot2 scale is what fails silently; passing the computed numbers works.
`scale_colour_intervals()` exists so you do not have to remember that.

## Palettes

### One syntax, five sources

```{r}
#| label: palette-sources
palette_sources()
as_palette("hcl::Zissou 1")(5)
as_palette("brewer::RdBu")(5)
as_palette("brewer::YlGnBu")(5)
as_palette(c("#1b1b3a", "#f2f2f2", "#b3001b"))(5)
```

`cols4all` and `paletteer` are optional. Install either and their names work in
the same place: `"c4a::hcl.blues3"`, `"scico::roma"`, `"MetBrewer::Hokusai1"`.

### Finding one

```{r}
#| label: palette-search
map_palettes("div") |> head(8)
map_palettes(source = "brewer", pattern = "^Yl")
nrow(map_palettes())
```

### Shaping one

`reverse` flips it, `range` trims the ends.

```{r}
#| label: palette-shaping
#| fig-height: 3.4
mw_map(scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlOrRd", "quantile", 5),
       var = "percbelowpoverty", title = "full ramp") +
  mw_map(scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlOrRd", "quantile", 5,
                              range = c(0.25, 1)),
         var = "percbelowpoverty", title = "range = c(0.25, 1)")
```

Trimming matters more than it sounds. The pale end of a sequential ramp is hard
to tell from the background and from a "no data" grey; `range = c(0.2, 1)` buys
back the distinction at almost no cost.

Ramp direction is the other thing worth checking before anything else. A
choropleth is read as *more ink means more of the thing*. ColorBrewer's
sequential palettes already run light to dark; viridis and its relatives run
dark to light, so on a map they need turning round.

```{r}
#| label: reverse
#| fig-height: 3.4
mw_map(scale_fill_intervals("viridis::mako", "quantile", 5),
       var = "percbelowpoverty", title = "mako as shipped: dark = low") +
  mw_map(scale_fill_intervals("viridis::mako", "quantile", 5, reverse = TRUE),
         var = "percbelowpoverty", title = "reverse = TRUE: dark = high")
```

## Diverging scales

Three things have to line up: a diverging palette, a `midpoint`, and limits that
are symmetric about it. `midpoint` also places a class break exactly on the
midpoint, so the neutral colour means what it looks like it means.

```{r}
#| label: diverging
#| fig-height: 3.4
mw_map(scale_fill_map("brewer::RdBu", midpoint = 0, reverse = TRUE),
       var = "college_gap", title = "midpoint = 0") +
  mw_map(scale_fill_map("brewer::RdBu", midpoint = 0, reverse = TRUE,
                        limits = symmetric_limits(0)),
         var = "college_gap", title = "+ symmetric_limits(0)")
```

```{r}
#| label: diverging-break
sc <- ggplot_build(
  mw_map(scale_fill_intervals("brewer::RdBu", "quantile", 6, midpoint = 0))
)$plot$scales$scales[[1]]
sc$frozen_breaks
0 %in% sc$frozen_breaks
```

## Limits, outliers and squishing

`oob = "squish"` is the default, which is the cartographic convention: a value
past the end of the scale joins the end class rather than disappearing.
`trim_limits()` sets the limits from quantiles, so one county cannot flatten
the whole ramp.

```{r}
#| label: limits
#| fig-height: 6.5
(
  mw_map(scale_fill_map("brewer::YlGnBu"), title = "full range") +
  mw_map(scale_fill_map("brewer::YlGnBu", limits = trim_limits(0.02, 0.95)),
         title = "trim_limits(0.02, 0.95), squished")
) / (
  mw_map(scale_fill_map("brewer::YlGnBu", limits = trim_limits(0.02, 0.95),
                        oob = "censor", na.value = "grey70"),
         title = 'oob = "censor"') +
  mw_map(scale_fill_map("brewer::YlGnBu", limits = c(0, 2e5)),
         title = "limits = c(0, 2e5)")
)
```

Squish and censor are a real choice, not a default to accept blindly. Squishing
keeps the map complete but hides how extreme the extreme is; censoring is
honest about the exclusion but leaves holes that read as missing data. If you
squish, say so in the legend — `label_map(open = TRUE)` writes
"and above" for you.

## Legend labels

```{r}
#| label: labels
#| fig-height: 6.5
(
  mw_map(scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", "quantile", 5),
         title = "default: break values") +
  mw_map(scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", "quantile", 5, labels = "ranges"),
         title = 'labels = "ranges"')
) / (
  mw_map(scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", "quantile", 5,
                              labels = label_map(style = "interval", open = TRUE,
                                                 scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k",
                                                 digits = 0)),
         title = "thousands, open ends") +
  mw_map(scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", "quantile", 5,
                              labels = label_map(style = "interval", suffix = "%",
                                                 digits = 1, separator = " - ")),
         var = "percbelowpoverty", title = "percent, custom separator")
)
```

`label_map()` on its own, outside any scale:

```{r}
#| label: label-map
label_map(prefix = "$", big.mark = ",", digits = 0)(c(1250, 48000, 1.2e6))
label_map(style = "interval", digits = 0)(c(0, 10, 25, 60))
label_map(style = "interval", open = TRUE, suffix = "%", digits = 1)(c(0, 10, 25, 60))
label_map(scale = 1/1e6, suffix = "M", digits = 2)(5105067)
```

## Missing data

```{r}
#| label: missing
#| fig-height: 3.4
holes <- mw_poly |>
  mutate(percollege = ifelse(region == "indiana" & sub < "e", NA, percollege))

gap_map <- function(sc, ttl) {
  ggplot(holes, aes(long, lat, group = group, fill = percollege)) +
    geom_polygon(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.07) +
    coord_quickmap() + sc + labs(title = ttl, fill = NULL) +
    theme_void(base_size = 9) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9.5),
          legend.key.size = unit(8, "pt"), legend.text = element_text(size = 6.5))
}

gap_map(scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", "quantile", 5,
                             na.value = "grey88"), "na.value = grey") +
  gap_map(scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", "quantile", 5,
                               na.value = "white"), "na.value = white")
```

Categorical scales get a labelled key for missing values:

```{r}
#| label: missing-cat
#| fig-height: 3.4
mw_poly |>
  mutate(size_class = cut(poptotal, breaks_fisher(4)(poptotal),
                          labels = c("small", "mid", "large", "metro"),
                          include.lowest = TRUE),
         size_class = ifelse(region == "wisconsin" & sub < "d", NA,
                             as.character(size_class))) |>
  ggplot(aes(long, lat, group = group, fill = size_class)) +
  geom_polygon(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.07) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  scale_fill_cat("brewer::YlGnBu", na.value = "grey88", na.label = "No data") +
  theme_void(9) + labs(fill = NULL)
```

On a continuous colourbar there is nowhere to put a "no data" key without a
custom guide; that is a known gap. For now, either use an interval scale — which
gets one — or annotate it yourself.

## How colours attach to classes

`interpolate = "even"` gives every class an evenly spaced colour, the way GIS
software does. `interpolate = "value"` places each class's colour at its
position along the data range, so a wide class sits further along the ramp.
On skewed data the difference is dramatic.

```{r}
#| label: interpolate
#| fig-height: 3.4
mw_map(scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", "quantile", 5, interpolate = "even"),
       title = 'interpolate = "even"') +
  mw_map(scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", "quantile", 5, interpolate = "value"),
         title = 'interpolate = "value"')
```

"even" is the right default for reading a map. "value" is the honest one if the
reader will treat colour as a continuous quantity.

## Two variables at once: bivariate maps

A bivariate choropleth shows two variables on one map by classing each into
`n` intervals and giving every one of the `n × n` combinations its own colour.
Three classes each is the convention; the legend is a 3 × 3 grid and the eye
can still tell the cells apart.

Three steps. Classify both variables into one factor:

```{r}
#| label: bivariate-classify
mw_poly <- mw_poly |>
  mutate(cls = classify_bivariate(percollege, percbelowpoverty, n = 3,
                                  style = "quantile"))
table(mw_poly$cls)
attr(mw_poly$cls, "breaks_x")
```

`style = "quantile"` is the usual choice here because it guarantees every row
and column of the legend has counties in it. Any style from `map_styles()`
works; `style_x` and `style_y` class the two variables differently, and
`trans_x` / `trans_y` class a skewed variable on, say, a log scale while
the stored breaks -- and therefore the legend -- stay in the original units:

```{r}
#| label: bivariate-trans
attr(classify_bivariate(mw_data$poptotal, mw_data$percollege, n = 3,
                        style_x = "equal", trans_x = "log10"), "breaks_x")
```

Colour the map with `scale_fill_bivariate()`, which keeps all nine classes
even if one is empty, so map and legend always agree:

```{r}
#| label: bivariate-map
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
bimap <- ggplot(mw_poly, aes(long, lat, group = group, fill = cls)) +
  geom_polygon(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  scale_fill_bivariate("purple-green", n = 3) +
  labs(title = "College attainment and poverty, Midwest counties") +
  theme_void()

legend <- legend_bivariate("purple-green", classes = mw_poly$cls,
                           style = "diamond", ends = FALSE, text_size = 8,
                           xlab = "% college", ylab = "% in poverty",
                           labels = label_map(digits = 0, suffix = "%"),
                           background = alpha("white", 0.85))

inset_legend(bimap, legend, position = "topleft", width = 0.36)
```

The scale draws no legend of its own; `legend_bivariate()` is a small ggplot
you place with `inset_legend()` (patchwork underneath) or beside the map with
`patchwork` / `cowplot`. Passing `classes = ` gives it the break points so
the grid edges carry real values; `ends = FALSE` drops the data minimum and
maximum from the labels, leaving only the cut points, which is what most
published maps show.

Two layouts. `style = "square"` has an arrowed axis on each side and reads
like a chart. `style = "diamond"` is the rotated grid newspapers use, with
both-low at the bottom and both-high at the top; values run along the two
lower edges, or `corner_labels` puts a short phrase at each corner and drops
the numbers altogether.

```{r}
#| label: bivariate-styles
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3
patchwork::wrap_plots(
  legend_bivariate("purple-green", 3, xlab = "Income", ylab = "% degree",
                   breaks_x = c(20, 40, 60, 90) * 1000,
                   breaks_y = c(5, 15, 25, 50),
                   labels = label_map(big.mark = ","), text_size = 10),
  legend_bivariate("blue-red", 4, style = "diamond",
                   xlab = "% Black", ylab = "% Hispanic",
                   breaks_x = c(0, 5, 20, 50, 95), breaks_y = c(0, 5, 20, 50, 95),
                   labels = label_map(suffix = "%"), text_size = 10),
  legend_bivariate("blue-yellow", 3, style = "diamond", text_size = 9,
                   corner_labels = c("Low diversity\nLittle change",
                                     "High diversity\nLittle change",
                                     "Low diversity\nBig increase",
                                     "High diversity\nBig increase")),
  nrow = 1
)
```

Palettes come from `bivariate_palettes()` -- corner presets that work at
any `n`, and the Stevens 3 × 3 grids (`"stevens-purpleblue"` ...) -- from
four corner colours or a full grid of your own, or from any two sequential
ramps the package already knows. `plot_bivariate_palettes()` draws them all.

```{r}
#| label: bivariate-palettes
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.6
pals <- list(
  legend_bivariate("blue-red", 3, "x", "y"),
  legend_bivariate("teal-pink", 3, "x", "y"),
  legend_bivariate(c("#f3f3f3", "steelblue", "firebrick", "#2b1b2b"), 4, "x", "y"),
  legend_bivariate(list(x = "brewer::Blues", y = "brewer::Reds"), 3, "x", "y")
)
patchwork::wrap_plots(pals, nrow = 1)
```

Reading a bivariate map takes practice, and readers only manage it when the
legend is close to the map, large enough to see, and labelled with the
variable names and their direction. `legend_bivariate()` does the last two by
default; `inset_legend()` handles the first.

## Project defaults

Set the palettes once and stop repeating yourself.

```{r}
#| label: defaults
#| fig-height: 3.2
old <- ggcarto_palettes(seq = "hcl::Batlow", div = "brewer::BrBG",
                        cat = "brewer::Dark2")

mw_map(scale_fill_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5), title = "no palette named") +
  mw_map(scale_fill_map(midpoint = 0), var = "college_gap",
         title = "no palette named, diverging")
```

On ggplot2 4.0 and later, `theme_palettes()` pushes the same choices into
ggplot2's own default scales, so unstyled layers match the ones you scale
explicitly.

```{r}
#| label: theme-palettes
#| fig-height: 3
ggplot(mw_data, aes(percollege, percbelowpoverty, colour = state)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  theme_minimal(9) +
  theme_palettes(cat = "brewer::Dark2")
```

```{r}
#| label: restore
options(ggcarto.palettes = old)
```

## Not only for maps

Nothing here is map-specific. Any skewed variable benefits, and the legend
niceties apply anywhere.

```{r}
#| label: nonmap
#| fig-height: 3.2
diamonds |>
  slice_sample(n = 4000) |>
  ggplot(aes(carat, price, colour = price)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_intervals("hcl::Batlow", style = "quantile", n = 6,
                         labels = label_map(style = "interval", prefix = "$",
                                            big.mark = ",", digits = 0)) +
  theme_minimal(9) +
  labs(colour = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: nonmap-heat
#| fig-height: 3.2
txhousing |>
  filter(!is.na(median)) |>
  summarise(median = median(median), .by = c(year, month)) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(month), factor(year), fill = median)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_intervals("viridis::rocket", style = "fisher", n = 7,
                       range = c(0.15, 0.95),
                       labels = label_map(scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k",
                                          style = "interval", digits = 0)) +
  labs(x = "month", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(9)
```

## Recipes

```r
# a plain choropleth you would not be embarrassed by
scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", style = "fisher", n = 6,
                     range = c(0.15, 1), na.value = "grey90",
                     labels = label_map(style = "interval", open = TRUE))

# money
scale_fill_intervals("hcl::Batlow", style = "quantile", n = 5,
                     labels = label_map(style = "interval", prefix = "$",
                                        big.mark = ",", digits = 0))

# a rate, diverging around the national figure
scale_fill_map("brewer::RdBu", midpoint = 6.2, reverse = TRUE,
               limits = symmetric_limits(6.2),
               labels = label_map(suffix = "%", digits = 1))

# counts with a long tail
scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", style = "headtails",
                     labels = label_map(style = "interval", big.mark = ","))

# outlier-proof, no thinking required
scale_fill_rank("brewer::YlGnBu")
```
